arXiv:2607.02534v1 [math.AP] 17 Jun 2026

Exact self-similar solutions for nonlinear coupled heat–elastic wave systems with temperature-dependent material properties

Manjit Singh ††thanks: corresponding author: manjitcsir@gmail.com    Radhika Affiliation: Yadavindra Department of Sciences, Punjabi University Guru Kashi Campus, Talwandi Sabo–151302, Punjab, India.
Abstract

In this work, we study a coupled nonlinear thermoelastic system in which the heat capacity, thermal conductivity, and elastic modulus are all temperature-dependent. The thermal conduction equation is formulated in a generalized radial geometry governed by a parameter ν\nu, which encompasses planar, cylindrical, and spherical configurations as special cases. A complete Lie symmetry classification of the admissible constitutive functions is carried out, yielding three principal classes: exponential laws, power laws, and a unified class that contains both as limiting cases. For each class, the admitted symmetry algebras are determined, optimal systems of one-dimensional subalgebras are constructed, and the governing partial differential equations are reduced to coupled ordinary differential equation systems via similarity transformations. Exact closed-form solutions are obtained for each class using a combination of integrating factor methods, flux-variable substitutions, and power-law and logarithmic ansätze. For the exponential class, the thermal field exhibits a logarithmic similarity profile while the displacement field decays algebraically, with the geometry parameter absorbed into the leading-order transformation. For the power-law class, the thermal field follows a self-similar power-law profile and the displacement field decomposes into distinct elastic, self-similar, and thermoelastically driven modes. Travelling-wave solutions are also constructed, with elementary forms recovered in limiting cases. The influence of geometry, particularly the structural distinction between cylindrical and other configurations, is identified and physically interpreted. All solutions are discussed in terms of the interplay between thermal diffusion, elastic stiffness, and thermoelastic coupling.

Keywords: Thermoelasticity, Lie symmetry analysis, group classification, optimal systems, similarity reductions, invariant solutions, constitutive functions.
MSC (2020): 35A30, 35B06, 35C06, 35K65, 74F05.
PACS numbers: 02.20.Sv, 02.30.Jr, 44.05.+e, 46.25.Hf

1 Introduction

The mutual interaction between heat conduction and mechanical deformation is a fundamental feature of many problems in continuum mechanics [1, 29, 8]. When a solid body is subjected to a thermal load, the resulting temperature gradients generate internal stresses that drive elastic displacements; conversely, rapid deformation produces local heating through the thermoelastic coupling term [3]. This two-way feedback is described by a coupled system of partial differential equations (PDEs) linking the temperature field u⁡(z,t)u(z,t) to the displacement field w⁡(z,t)w(z,t). Classical linear thermoelasticity, as formulated by Biot [1] and surveyed by Nowacki [17], assumes constant material parameters and admits Fourier-series or integral transform solutions. However, in many physically relevant situations, the material coefficients strongly depend on the temperature. High-temperature aerospace applications, geothermal processes in porous rocks, and thermal therapies in biological tissues frequently involve material properties whose thermal and mechanical characteristics exhibit significant temperature dependence. Consequently, the assumption of constant conductivity, heat capacity, and elastic modulus may no longer be adequate for accurate thermoelastic modelling [13, 26, 16]. In such regimes, linear theory breaks down and the governing equations become nonlinear and coupled in an essential way.

Exact analytical solutions of nonlinear PDE systems are of particular value: they provide benchmark data for numerical solvers, reveal the dominant physical balance governing a given regime, and expose the role of constitutive nonlinearity in a transparent form that parameter studies cannot easily replicate [23, 5, 24, 11, 10, 25].

Self-similar and travelling-wave solutions, more generally group-invariant solutions, constitute an important class of exact solutions for coupled thermoelastic systems, since they reduce the governing partial differential equations to ordinary differential equations in suitable invariant variables. The existence of such reductions depends critically on the constitutive functions C⁡(u)C(u), K⁡(u)K(u), E⁡(u)E(u). For arbitrary material laws, nontrivial similarity reductions are generally not available. Consequently, the determination of all constitutive classes admitting additional symmetry generators becomes a group-classification problem, whose solution provides the foundation for the systematic construction of invariant solutions [22, 12, 28, 15]. This is the approach adopted in the present work. The governing system considered here takes the form

C⁡(u)​ut\displaystyle C(u)\,u_{t} =1zν​(K⁡(u)​zν​uz)z+γ​wt,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{z^{\nu}}\left(K(u)\,z^{\nu}u_{z}\right)_{z}+\gamma\,w_{t}, (1)
ρ​wt​t\displaystyle\rho\,w_{tt} =(E⁡(u)​wz)z+β​uz.\displaystyle=\left(E(u)\,w_{z}\right)_{z}+\beta\,u_{z}.

Here u=u⁡(z,t)u=\,u(z,t) is the temperature or thermal field, w=w⁡(z,t)w=\,w(z,t) is the displacement field, E⁡(u)E(u) is the temperature dependent elastic modulus, β​uz\beta\,u_{z} is the thermoelastic forcing caused by temperature gradients, the term (E⁡(u)​wz)z\left(E(u)\,w_{z}\right)_{z} implies that the local stiffness changes with temperature. The parameter ν\nu enters the thermal conduction equation because the heat diffuses through cross-sectional areas that scale like zνz^{\nu} and it enters only in the first equation of the model (1). The second equation looks like a one-dimensional axial elastic wave equation. It describes displacement along a straight coordinate zz, without a radial divergence operator.

Despite the extensive literature on thermoelasticity and symmetry methods for differential equations, a complete group classification of the thermoelastic system with arbitrary temperature-dependent constitutive functions C⁡(u),K⁡(u)C(u),K(u), and E⁡(u)E(u) appears to be absent from the literature. The primary objective of the present work is to fill this gap by determining all constitutive classes that lead to extensions of the principal Lie invariance algebra, recovering three main classes together with their admitted symmetry algebras and optimal systems of one-dimensional subalgebras. For selected representative subalgebra, the corresponding similarity or travelling-wave reduction is performed and the resulting ODE system is solved explicitly or in terms of standard special functions. The classification of constitutive functions that admit symmetry extensions of the principal algebra is then carried out.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. section 2 presents the constitutive classification together with the admitted symmetry algebras. section 3 constructs optimal systems of one-dimensional subalgebras for each algebra. section 4 derives the similarity variables and the reduced ODE systems corresponding to selected generators. section 5 constructs the group-invariant solutions and discusses their physical interpretation. Finally, section 6 and section 7 present general observations and concluding remarks, respectively.

2 Lie symmetries

We seek the Lie point symmetries admitted by the following thermoelastic system:

C⁡(u)​ut\displaystyle C(u)\,u_{t} =K⁡(u)​uz​z+K′​(u)​uz2+νz​K​(u)​uz+γ​wt,\displaystyle=K(u)\,u_{zz}+K^{\prime}(u)\,u_{z}^{2}+\frac{\nu}{z}\,K(u)\,u_{z}+\gamma\,w_{t}, (2)
ρ​wt​t\displaystyle\rho\,w_{tt} =E⁡(u)​wz​z+E′​(u)​uz​wz+β​uz.\displaystyle=E(u)\,w_{zz}+E^{\prime}(u)u_{z}w_{z}+\beta\,u_{z}.

A one-parameter Lie group of point transformations acting on the space (z,t,u,w)(z,t,u,w) is generated by a vector field of the form

𝒳=ξ(z,t,u,w)∂z+τ(z,t,u,w)∂t+η(z,t,u,w)∂u+ϕ(z,t,u,w)∂w.\mathcal{X}=\xi(z,t,u,w)\,\partial_{z}+\tau(z,t,u,w)\,\partial_{t}+\eta(z,t,u,w)\,\partial_{u}+\phi(z,t,u,w)\,\partial_{w}. (3)

The system (2) admits 𝒳\mathcal{X} as a symmetry generator if and only if the second prolongation pr(2)​𝒳\text{pr}^{(2)}\mathcal{X} annihilates each equation on the solution manifold, i.e.,

pr(2)𝒳(Δi)|Δi=0=0,i=1,2,\left.\text{pr}^{(2)}\mathcal{X}(\Delta_{i})\right|_{\Delta_{i}=0}=0,\qquad i=1,2, (4)

where Δi=0\Delta_{i}=0 denotes the ii-th equation of the system. Applying this invariance condition and equating coefficients of the independent derivative monomials to zero yields an overdetermined system of linear PDEs in the unknowns ξ,τ,η,ϕ\xi,\tau,\eta,\phi, known as the determining equations. The computation of the prolonged invariance conditions and the subsequent derivation of the determining equations are entirely standard within the framework of Lie group analysis. Therefore, only the final determining equations are presented below; further details of the procedure may be found in the classical references [19, 20, 2].

ξt= 0,ξu= 0,ξw= 0,\displaystyle\xi_{t}=\,0,\;\xi_{u}=\,0,\;\xi_{w}=\,0, (5a)
τu= 0,τw= 0,τz= 0,\displaystyle\tau_{u}=\,0,\;\tau_{w}=\,0,\;\tau_{z}=\,0, (5b)
ηw= 0,ϕu= 0,\displaystyle\eta_{w}=\,0,\;\phi_{u}=\,0, (5c)

K⁡(u)​η​CuC⁡(u)+2​K​(u)​ξz−τt​K​(u)−η​Ku=0,\displaystyle\frac{K(u)\,\eta\,C_{u}}{C(u)}+2K(u)\,\xi_{z}-\tau_{t}\,K(u)-\eta\,K_{u}=0, (5e)
ηt​C​(u)−ηz​ν​K​(u)z−ϕt​γ−ηz,z​K​(u)=0,\displaystyle\eta_{t}\,C(u)-\frac{\eta_{z}\,\nu\,K(u)}{z}-\phi_{t}\,\gamma-\eta_{z,z}\,K(u)=0, (5f)

ϕw,w=0,\displaystyle\phi_{w,w}=0, (5i)

Our objective is therefore to determine all admissible forms of C⁡(u),K⁡(u)C(u),K(u) and E⁡(u)E(u) together with their corresponding Lie symmetry generators. The determining equations (5a)-(5c) give

ηz=ηt=0,a⁡(z)=a0,τ⁡(t)=c1​t+c0.\eta_{z}=\eta_{t}=0,\qquad a(z)=a_{0},\qquad\tau(t)=c_{1}t+c_{0}. (31)

These are only the translational symmetries in tt and ww. Since our aim is to obtain an enlargement of the admitted symmetry algebra, this generic branch is not suitable for further reduction. Therefore, in the following analysis, we look for special constitutive classes of C⁡(u)C(u), K⁡(u)K(u) and E⁡(u)E(u) for which additional symmetries are admitted.

Non-kernel classifications

For non-kernel symmetries, we assume η≠0.\eta\neq 0. The principal classifying equations (5d), (5e) and (5l) imply that the quantities

12​τt+a⁡(z)−ηuη,a⁡(z)+2​ξz−12​τt−ηuη,2​ξz−2​τtη,\frac{\frac{1}{2}\tau_{t}+a(z)-\eta_{u}}{\eta},\qquad\frac{a(z)+2\xi_{z}-\frac{1}{2}\tau_{t}-\eta_{u}}{\eta},\qquad\frac{2\xi_{z}-2\tau_{t}}{\eta}, (34)

must each depend on the variable uu alone.

Therefore, the existence of non-kernel symmetries requires special constitutive functions C⁡(u)C(u), K⁡(u)K(u), and E⁡(u)E(u). The standard non-kernel symmetry classes arise when the infinitesimal η\eta is affine in uu, namely

η=α​u+δ,\eta=\alpha u+\delta, (35)

where α\alpha and δ\delta are constants.

Case 2.1.

In what follows we assume β≠0\beta\neq 0. The displayed algebras are written for γ≠0\gamma\neq 0. If γ=0\gamma=0, the additional kernel generator t∂wt\partial_{w} must be included. The branch of non-constant elasticity Eu≠0E_{u}\neq 0 implies that

T=p+q3,A=2​q−p3,r=2​q−4​p3,a0=5​p−q6.T=\frac{p+q}{3},\qquad A=\frac{2q-p}{3},\qquad r=\frac{2q-4p}{3},\qquad a_{0}=\frac{5p-q}{6}. (43)

𝒳(1)=2​q−p3z∂z+p+q3t∂t+∂u+pw∂w.\mathcal{X}^{(1)}=\frac{2q-p}{3}z\partial_{z}+\frac{p+q}{3}t\partial_{t}+\partial_{u}+pw\partial_{w}. (44)

Case 2.2.

We next consider the power-law ansatz

η=u,C=C0​up,K=K0​uq,E=E0​ur.\eta=u,\qquad C=C_{0}u^{p},\qquad K=K_{0}u^{q},\qquad E=E_{0}u^{r}. (47)

𝒳(2)=pz∂z+pt∂t+u∂u+(p+1)w∂w,\mathcal{X}^{(2)}=pz\partial_{z}+pt\partial_{t}+u\partial_{u}+(p+1)w\partial_{w}, (53)

Case 2.3.

𝒳(3)=pz∂z+pt∂t+(qu+n)∂u+(p+q)w∂w.\mathcal{X}^{(3)}=pz\partial_{z}+pt\partial_{t}+(qu+n)\partial_{u}+(p+q)w\partial_{w}. (66)

This subclass contains both the exponential and power-law symmetry extensions as special cases. Hence, it provides a unified constitutive framework for both exponential and power-law branches of the constant elasticity case.

3 Optimal systems of subalgebras

In the preceding section, several finite-dimensional Lie algebras admitted by the thermo-elastic model were obtained for different choices of the constitutive functions and for different values of the parameter ν\nu. Each admitted algebra generates a local Lie group of point transformations under which the governing system remains invariant. If a solution is invariant under a subgroup HH of the full admitted symmetry group GG, then the transformed solution obtained by applying an element g∈Gg\in G is invariant under the conjugate subgroup g​H​g−1gHg^{-1}. Hence, two reductions associated with conjugate subgroups are equivalent and need not be considered separately. The purpose of constructing an optimal system is therefore to obtain a minimal list of mutually inequivalent subalgebras, one representative from each conjugacy class.

It is convenient to formulate this equivalence at the level of the Lie algebra. If V,W∈𝔤V,W\in\mathfrak{g}, then the adjoint action of the one-parameter group generated by VV on WW is given by

Ad⁡(exp⁡(ε​V))​W=W−ε⁡[V,W]+ε22​[V,[V,W]]−⋯.\operatorname{Ad}\left(\exp(\varepsilon V)\right)W=W-\varepsilon[V,W]+\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{2}[V,[V,W]]-\cdots. (69)

Consequently, the adjoint transformations required for the construction of the optimal system can be derived directly from the non-vanishing commutation relations of the admitted algebra. The methodology for constructing optimal systems through the adjoint representation is well established in the Lie symmetry literature; see, for instance, [20, 19, 4, 14].

For the thermo-elastic model, we shall apply this procedure separately to each admitted algebra. In the case ν≠0\nu\neq 0, the admitted algebra is

𝔤1(1)=⟨T,W,𝒳(1)⟩,T=∂t,W=∂w,\mathfrak{g}^{(1)}_{1}=\left\langle T,W,\mathcal{X}^{(1)}\right\rangle,\qquad T=\partial_{t},\quad W=\partial_{w}, (70)

where

𝒳(1)=2​q−p3z∂z+p+q3t∂t+∂u+pw∂w.\mathcal{X}^{(1)}=\frac{2q-p}{3}z\partial_{z}+\frac{p+q}{3}t\partial_{t}+\partial_{u}+pw\partial_{w}. (71)

For ν=0\nu=0, the additional translation

Z=∂zZ=\partial_{z}

is admitted, and the algebra becomes

𝔤1(2)=⟨T,Z,W,𝒳(1)⟩.\mathfrak{g}^{(2)}_{1}=\left\langle T,Z,W,\mathcal{X}^{(1)}\right\rangle. (72)

The optimal classification will be obtained by taking a general element of the corresponding algebra, simplifying its coefficients through the adjoint transformations, and retaining only inequivalent representatives.

It should also be observed that any generator which commutes with all elements of the algebra belongs to the center. Such central elements are invariant under the adjoint action and therefore cannot be removed by conjugation. Their presence must be recorded explicitly in the optimal system, usually through arbitrary constants attached to the representatives. This point is especially relevant when translations such as

T=∂t,Z=∂z,W=∂w,T=\partial_{t},\qquad Z=\partial_{z},\qquad W=\partial_{w},

commute with other admitted generators for special parameter choices.

Hence, the construction of the optimal system proceeds in three steps: first, compute the commutator table of the admitted algebra; second, derive the corresponding adjoint transformations using the commutator expansion (69); and third, act on a general linear combination of generators in order to reduce it to a simplest canonical representative. The resulting list gives the one-dimensional optimal system of subalgebras and consequently provides the inequivalent symmetry reductions of the thermo-elastic equations.

Optimal classification of 𝔤1(1)\mathfrak{g}^{(1)}_{1} For ν≠0\nu\neq 0, the nonzero commutators are

[𝒳(1),∂t]=−p+q3∂t,[𝒳(1),∂w]=−p∂w.[\mathcal{X}^{(1)},\partial_{t}]=-\frac{p+q}{3}\partial_{t},\qquad[\mathcal{X}^{(1)},\partial_{w}]=-p\partial_{w}.

Therefore, using the adjoint representation (69), the one-dimensional subalgebras of 𝔤1(1)\mathfrak{g}^{(1)}_{1} are classified up to conjugacy. 𝒪1(1)={⟨𝒳(1)⟩,⟨∂t⟩,⟨∂w⟩,⟨∂t+ε∂w⟩},ε=±1.\mathcal{O}^{(1)}_{1}=\left\{\left\langle\mathcal{X}^{(1)}\right\rangle,\;\left\langle\partial_{t}\right\rangle,\;\left\langle\partial_{w}\right\rangle,\;\left\langle\partial_{t}+\varepsilon\partial_{w}\right\rangle\right\},\qquad\varepsilon=\pm 1.

4 Similarity Variables and Reduced System

The principal application of the Lie point symmetries obtained in the preceding section is the construction of exact group-invariant solutions. Such solutions remain unchanged under the action of a one-parameter transformation group generated by an admitted symmetry vector field [20, 9, 2, 6, 27, 7]. Consequently, instead of depending on the original independent variables, they can be represented in terms of quantities that are invariant under the corresponding group action; such invariants can be derived from the following characteristic system:

d​zξ=d​tτ=d​uη=d​wϕ.\frac{dz}{\xi}=\frac{dt}{\tau}=\frac{du}{\eta}=\frac{dw}{\phi}. (73)

The functionally independent first integrals of the characteristic system described above (73) define the similarity variables. Expressing the dependent variables in terms of these invariants yields the associated similarity transformations. Substituting these similarity transformations into the governing equations replaces the original independent variables with the invariants of the symmetry group. Since the solution is constant along the group orbits generated by 𝒳\mathcal{X}, the dependence on one independent variable is eliminated. Consequently, a one-dimensional symmetry generator reduces the number of independent variables by one.

For the present thermo-elastic model, the independent variables are zz and tt. Therefore, each one-dimensional symmetry admitted by the model transforms the original system of partial differential equations into a coupled system of ordinary differential equations in a single similarity variable. Solving the reduced ordinary differential system then yields exact group-invariant solutions of the original thermo-elastic equations. In the following, we present similarity reduction for selected elements from 𝒪j(i)\mathcal{O}^{(i)}_{j}.

Reduction corresponding to 𝒳(1)∈𝒪1(1)\mathcal{X}^{(1)}\in\mathcal{O}^{(1)}_{1}. For

𝒳(1)=Az∂z+Bt∂t+∂u+pw∂w,A=2​q−p3,B=p+q3,\mathcal{X}^{(1)}=Az\partial_{z}+Bt\partial_{t}+\partial_{u}+pw\partial_{w},\quad A=\frac{2q-p}{3},\quad B=\frac{p+q}{3},

assuming B≠0B\neq 0, the characteristic system (73) gives

s=zt−A/B,u=1Blnt+F(s),w=tp/BG(s).s=zt^{-A/B},\qquad u=\frac{1}{B}\ln t+F(s),\qquad w=t^{p/B}G(s).

Equivalently,

s=z​t−α,u=δ​ln⁡t+F⁡(s),w=tσ​G​(s),s=zt^{-\alpha},\qquad u=\delta\ln t+F(s),\qquad w=t^{\sigma}G(s),

where

α=2​q−pp+q,δ=3p+q,σ=3​pp+q.\alpha=\frac{2q-p}{p+q},\qquad\delta=\frac{3}{p+q},\qquad\sigma=\frac{3p}{p+q}.

C=C0​ep​u,K=K0​eq​u,E=E0​er​u,r=2​q−4​p3,C=C_{0}e^{pu},\qquad K=K_{0}e^{qu},\qquad E=E_{0}e^{ru},\qquad r=\frac{2q-4p}{3},

C0​ep​F​(δ−α​s​F′)=K0​s−ν​(sν​eq​F​F′)′+γ⁡(σ​G−α​s​G′),\displaystyle C_{0}e^{pF}\left(\delta-\alpha sF^{\prime}\right)=K_{0}s^{-\nu}\left(s^{\nu}e^{qF}F^{\prime}\right)^{\prime}+\gamma\left(\sigma G-\alpha sG^{\prime}\right), (74)
ρ⁡[σ⁡(σ−1)​G−α​s​(2​σ−α−1)​G′+α2​s2​G′′]=E0​(er​F​G′)′+β​F′.\displaystyle\rho\left[\sigma(\sigma-1)G-\alpha s(2\sigma-\alpha-1)G^{\prime}+\alpha^{2}s^{2}G^{\prime\prime}\right]=E_{0}\left(e^{rF}G^{\prime}\right)^{\prime}+\beta F^{\prime}. (75)

5 Group invariant solutions

To illustrate the physical significance of the reduced system (74)–(75), we consider a set of standard thermoelastic parameters corresponding to a homogeneous isotropic medium. In particular, we assume

β=γ=ρ=K0=E0=C0=1,ν=1,p=q=r=1,δ=0.\beta=\gamma=\rho=K_{0}=E_{0}=C_{0}=1,\qquad\nu=1,\qquad p=q=r=1,\qquad\delta=0.

Here, β>0\beta>0 represents the thermoelastic coupling coefficient, γ>0\gamma>0 characterizes the feedback of the elastic field into the thermal equation, ρ\rho is the material density, while K0K_{0}, E0E_{0}, and C0C_{0} denote the reference thermal conductivity, elastic modulus, and heat capacity, respectively [17, 21, 18]. The choice ν=1\nu=1 corresponds to the standard radial geometry, whereas p=q=r=1p=q=r=1 yields the simplest linear constitutive laws, and δ=0\delta=0 excludes logarithmic corrections in the constitutive functions. Under these physically relevant assumptions, the reduced system (74)–(75) takes the form

eF​(−α​s​F′)=1s​(s​eF​F′)′+σ​G−α​s​G′,\displaystyle e^{F}(-\alpha sF^{\prime})=\frac{1}{s}\!\left(s\,e^{F}F^{\prime}\right)^{\prime}+\sigma G-\alpha sG^{\prime}, (91)
σ⁡(σ−1)​G−α​s​(2​σ−α−1)​G′+α2​s2​G′′=(eF​G′)′+F′.\displaystyle\sigma(\sigma-1)G-\alpha s(2\sigma-\alpha-1)G^{\prime}+\alpha^{2}s^{2}G^{\prime\prime}=\left(e^{F}G^{\prime}\right)^{\prime}+F^{\prime}. (92)

To further simplify the reduced system (91)–(92), we employ the logarithmic ansatz

F⁡(s)=a​ln⁡s,F(s)=a\ln s,

where aa is an arbitrary constant. This choice transforms the exponential term according to eF=sae^{F}=s^{a}, thus converting the system into a purely algebraic-differential form. Consequently, (91)–(92) reduce to

−α​a​sa=a2​sa−2+σ​G−α​s​G′,\displaystyle-\alpha a\,s^{a}=a^{2}s^{a-2}+\sigma G-\alpha sG^{\prime}, (93)
σ⁡(σ−1)​G−α​s​(2​σ−α−1)​G′+α2​s2​G′′=a​sa−1​G′+sa​G′′+as.\displaystyle\sigma(\sigma-1)G-\alpha s(2\sigma-\alpha-1)G^{\prime}+\alpha^{2}s^{2}G^{\prime\prime}=as^{a-1}G^{\prime}+s^{a}G^{\prime\prime}+\frac{a}{s}. (94)

For consistent power scaling, the terms in the reduced equations should be arranged so that incompatible powers of ss do not obstruct the solution procedure. Since the term a2​sa−2a^{2}s^{a-2} in (93) cannot directly balance the term −α​a​sa-\alpha as^{a} for the same power of ss, we choose a=2a=2, thus,

F⁡(s)=2​ln⁡s=ln⁡s2,eF=s2,F′=2s.F(s)=2\ln s=\ln s^{2},\qquad e^{F}=s^{2},\qquad F^{\prime}=\frac{2}{s}.

With this choice, (93) and (94) reduce to

−2​α​s2=4+σ​G−α​s​G′,\displaystyle-2\alpha s^{2}=4+\sigma G-\alpha sG^{\prime}, (95)
(α2−1)​s2​G′′−{α⁡(2​σ−α−1)+2}​s​G′+σ⁡(σ−1)​G=2s.\displaystyle(\alpha^{2}-1)s^{2}G^{\prime\prime}-\{\alpha(2\sigma-\alpha-1)+2\}sG^{\prime}+\sigma(\sigma-1)G=\frac{2}{s}. (96)

To further simplify the reduced system, we choose

α=1,\alpha=1,

which corresponds to the natural self-similar scaling of the model. From a physical viewpoint, this normalization may be interpreted as taking the characteristic thermoelastic wave speed to be unity.

With this choice, the coefficient of the highest-order derivative term in (96) vanishes since

α2−1=0.\alpha^{2}-1=0.

Consequently, the second-order equation reduces to the first-order linear ordinary differential equation

−2​σ​s​G′+σ⁡(σ−1)​G=2s.-2\sigma sG^{\prime}+\sigma(\sigma-1)G=\frac{2}{s}.

Assuming σ≠0\sigma\neq 0, division by σ\sigma yields

−2​s​G′+(σ−1)​G=2σ​s.-2sG^{\prime}+(\sigma-1)G=\frac{2}{\sigma s}. (97)

Equation (97) is a first-order linear differential equation for G⁡(s)G(s), which can be solved explicitly by the method of integrating factors. The solution is obtained as follows:

G⁡(s)=2σ⁡(σ+1)​s−1+C1​s(σ−1)/2.G(s)=\frac{2}{\sigma(\sigma+1)}\,s^{-1}+C_{1}s^{(\sigma-1)/2}. (98)

To ensure that the similarity solution remains bounded at infinity, we impose the decay condition

G⁡(s)→0,s→∞.G(s)\to 0,\qquad s\to\infty.

Since the particular solution behaves like s−1s^{-1}, it already vanishes as s→∞s\to\infty. Therefore, boundedness requires only that the homogeneous contribution s(σ−1)/2s^{(\sigma-1)/2} decay, which yields

σ<1.\sigma<1.

Substituting the solution

G⁡(s)=2σ⁡(σ+1)​s−1+C1​s(σ−1)/2G(s)=\frac{2}{\sigma(\sigma+1)}\,s^{-1}+C_{1}s^{(\sigma-1)/2}

into (95), and taking the physically admissible value α=1\alpha=1, yields

−2​s2=4+σ​G−s​G′.-2s^{2}=4+\sigma G-sG^{\prime}.

For the particular choice σ=12\sigma=\tfrac{1}{2}, one obtains

−2s2=4+4s−1+3​C14s−1/4.-2s^{2}=4+4s^{-1}+\frac{3C_{1}}{4}s^{-1/4}.

This relation cannot be satisfied identically for all ss. Instead, it should be interpreted as an asymptotic solvability condition, with the dominant balance governing the outer similarity region. Hence, the logarithmic ansatz

F⁡(s)=2​ln⁡sF(s)=2\ln s

provides the leading-order outer solution, while a separate inner expansion would be required to describe the behavior near s=0s=0. Since the logarithmic ansatz yields only the outer similarity behaviour, the solution in the neighbourhood of s=0s=0 must be treated separately. Assuming a regular Frobenius-type expansion, both F⁡(s)F(s) and G⁡(s)G(s) remain finite as s→0s\to 0, so that the inner solution is characterized by bounded thermal and elastic fields. Thus, the complete similarity solution consists of an outer logarithmic profile matched with a regular inner expansion near the origin. Thus, for for α=1,σ=12,a=2\alpha=1,\sigma=\frac{1}{2},a=2, we obtain

F(s)=2lns+F0,G(s)=83s−1+C1s−1/4.F(s)=2\ln s+F_{0},\qquad G(s)=\frac{8}{3}s^{-1}+C_{1}s^{-1/4}.

Imposing regularity of the elastic displacement removes the singular homogeneous contribution, so that C1=0C_{1}=0. Hence

G⁡(s)=83​s.G(s)=\frac{8}{3s}.

Therefore, using s=z​t−1s=zt^{-1}, the corresponding physical fields are

u⁡(z,t)= 2​ln⁡z−2​ln⁡t+F0,w⁡(z,t)=83​t3/2z\displaystyle u(z,t)=\,2\ln z-2\ln t+F_{0},\quad w(z,t)=\,\frac{8}{3}\frac{t^{3/2}}{z} (99)

The profiles obtained possess a clear thermo-elastic interpretation: the logarithmic behavior of u⁡(z,t)u(z,t) describes the dominant diffusive evolution of the thermal field, while displacement w⁡(z,t)w(z,t) represents a spatially localized elastic disturbance whose amplitude decreases away from the origin. Since the elastic field exhibits singular behavior near z=0z=0, the solution is naturally interpreted to describe the outer region of the medium, with a separate regular inner expansion required in the vicinity of the origin. It should therefore be emphasized that the reconstructed functions u⁡(z,t)u(z,t) and w⁡(z,t)w(z,t) are not exact similarity solutions of the original thermo-elastic system; rather, they constitute a leading-order outer asymptotic similarity solution capturing the principal balance between thermal diffusion and elastic deformation in the far-field regime.

It is worth noting that the above construction remains essentially unchanged for the spherical case (ν=2)(\nu=2). Indeed, the parameter ν\nu enters only through the radial diffusion term in the original thermal equation and does not explicitly appear in the reduced elastic equation. Moreover, the logarithmic similarity ansatz converts the radial operator into the same Euler–Cauchy type structure for both ν=1\nu=1 and ν=2\nu=2. Consequently, the reduction procedure effectively absorbs the geometric contribution of ν\nu into the similarity transformation, so that the resulting leading-order outer asymptotic similarity solution retains the same functional form in both the cylindrical and spherical geometries.

The reduced system (80)–(81) remains nonlinear and coupled. In general, obtaining its complete solution appears difficult. However, the structure of (80) suggests the possibility of self-similar power-law solutions, since all terms involve products of powers of (F)(F) and its derivatives. Motivated by this observation, we seek a particular solution of the form F⁡(s)=A​sμF(s)=As^{\mu}, where AA and μ\mu are constants to be determined. Substitution into (80) allows the powers of the similarity variable (s)(s) to be balanced, leading to an algebraic determination of the exponent μ\mu. Once the thermal profile F⁡(s)F(s) is obtained, equation (80) becomes a nonhomogeneous linear ordinary differential equation for the displacement function G⁡(s)G(s), whose coefficients are completely determined by the known thermal field. Consequently, the thermoelastic problem can be solved sequentially: first, the thermal equation is solved for FF, after which the resulting expression is substituted into the mechanical equation to determine GG. K⁡(u)=K0​u2​p=K0.K(u)=K_{0}u^{2p}=K_{0}.

Thus, the thermal conductivity is constant and the governing heat-conduction equation becomes linear. In this case the general solution simplifies considerably, since F2​p+1=FF^{2p+1}=F and therefore the auxiliary variable satisfies Ψ=F\Psi=F. The temperature profile is obtained directly as

F⁡(z)=A2−λ0​z2,λ0=γ​ε2​K0​(ν+1).F(z)=A_{2}-\lambda_{0}z^{2},\qquad\lambda_{0}=\frac{\gamma\varepsilon}{2K_{0}(\nu+1)}. (117)

Substituting this expression into the reduced displacement equation yields

G′​(z)=1E0​[B1−β⁡(A2−λ0​z2)].G^{\prime}(z)=\frac{1}{E_{0}}\left[B_{1}-\beta\left(A_{2}-\lambda_{0}z^{2}\right)\right].

A further integration gives the explicit displacement field

G⁡(z)=1E0​[(B1−β​A2)​z+β​λ03​z3]+B2.G(z)=\frac{1}{E_{0}}\left[(B_{1}-\beta A_{2})z+\frac{\beta\lambda_{0}}{3}z^{3}\right]+B_{2}. (118)

Consequently, the invariant solution takes the form

u⁡(z,t)\displaystyle u(z,t) =A2−λ0​z2,\displaystyle=A_{2}-\lambda_{0}z^{2}, (119)
w⁡(z,t)\displaystyle w(z,t) =ε​t+1E0​[(B1−β​A2)​z+β​λ03​z3]+B2.\displaystyle=\varepsilon t+\frac{1}{E_{0}}\left[(B_{1}-\beta A_{2})z+\frac{\beta\lambda_{0}}{3}z^{3}\right]+B_{2}. (120)

Unlike the general nonlinear case, where the displacement field is expressed through a hypergeometric function, the constant-conductivity model admits elementary polynomial solutions. This case therefore provides a useful benchmark against which the behaviour of solutions corresponding to nonlinear conductivity laws (p≠0p\neq 0) may be compared.

Special case p=1p=1.

When p=1p=1, the conductivity law becomes

K⁡(u)=K0​u2,K(u)=K_{0}u^{2},

and the auxiliary variable is Ψ=F3\Psi=F^{3}. Consequently, the temperature profile takes the form

F⁡(z)=(A2−λ​z2)1/3.F(z)=\left(A_{2}-\lambda z^{2}\right)^{1/3}. (121)

The corresponding displacement field is expressed through the Gauss hypergeometric function

F12​(12,−13,32,ξ2).{}_{2}F_{1}\!\left(\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{3};\frac{3}{2};\xi^{2}\right).

Unlike the case p=0p=0, this function does not reduce to elementary functions for general values of zz. Nevertheless, a useful approximation may be obtained near the origin by expanding the hypergeometric function into a power series. This yields

G⁡(z)≈1E0​[B1​z−β​A21/3​(z−λ​z35​A2−λ2​z540​A22−⋯)]+B2.G(z)\approx\frac{1}{E_{0}}\left[B_{1}z-\beta A_{2}^{1/3}\left(z-\frac{\lambda z^{3}}{5A_{2}}-\frac{\lambda^{2}z^{5}}{40A_{2}^{2}}-\cdots\right)\right]+B_{2}. (122)

Thus, for quadratic conductivity, the temperature field remains available in closed form, whereas the displacement field is represented by a hypergeometric function whose local behaviour is described by the above asymptotic expansion.

Limiting case p→∞p\to\infty.

As p→∞p\to\infty, the exponent satisfies

12​p+1→0.\frac{1}{2p+1}\to 0.

Consequently,

F⁡(z)=(A2−λ​z2)12​p+1⟶(A2−λ​z2)0=1,F(z)=\left(A_{2}-\lambda z^{2}\right)^{\frac{1}{2p+1}}\longrightarrow\left(A_{2}-\lambda z^{2}\right)^{0}=1,

corresponding to a spatially uniform temperature field. Substituting this result into the reduced displacement equation yields

G′​(z)=B1−βE0,G^{\prime}(z)=\frac{B_{1}-\beta}{E_{0}},

which is constant. A further integration gives

G⁡(z)=B1−βE0​z+B2.G(z)=\frac{B_{1}-\beta}{E_{0}}\,z+B_{2}. (123)

Hence, in the limit p→∞p\to\infty, the invariant solution reduces to

u⁡(z,t)\displaystyle u(z,t) =1,\displaystyle=1, (124)
w⁡(z,t)\displaystyle w(z,t) =ε​t+B1−βE0​z+B2.\displaystyle=\varepsilon t+\frac{B_{1}-\beta}{E_{0}}\,z+B_{2}. (125)

In the limiting case p→∞p\to\infty, the temperature profile approaches a spatially uniform state, while the displacement field becomes linear in the spatial variable zz. Physically, this behaviour suggests that increasingly strong temperature-dependent conductivity suppresses thermal gradients, thereby driving the thermoelastic system toward an isothermal regime.

The reduced system associated with ∂t+ε1∂w+ε2z∂w∈𝒪(1)3\partial_{t}+\varepsilon_{1}\partial_{w}+\varepsilon_{2}z\partial_{w}\in\mathcal{O}^{(1)}_{3} is omitted from the list of explicit solutions because it is obtained by exactly the same quadrature procedure as the preceding case. The affine forcing term ε1+ε2​z\varepsilon_{1}+\varepsilon_{2}z only adds an extra polynomial contribution to the flux variable Ψ=F2​p+1\Psi=F^{2p+1} and does not change the structure of the solution. The displacement component is subsequently determined from the same equation E0​G′′+β​F′=0E_{0}G^{\prime\prime}+\beta F^{\prime}=0. Hence no essentially new invariant solution is obtained, apart from a direct polynomial modification of the previously derived family.

For completeness, invariant reductions corresponding to the remaining generators of the optimal system can be derived in exactly the same fashion. However, the resulting reduced ordinary differential equations do not introduce new analytical features and are solved by the same techniques as those employed above. Consequently, only representative cases are discussed in detail, as they adequately demonstrate the reduction procedure and the construction of exact solutions.

6 Observations and limitations of the study

The present work focuses on leading-order outer similarity solutions valid in the far-field regime s≫1s\gg 1, where the principal balance between thermal diffusion and elastic restoring terms is achieved; the construction of a matched inner expansion describing the neighbourhood of the source, which would complete the composite asymptotic picture, falls outside the scope of a single study of this breadth.

The power-law similarity solutions are derived for generic values of the constitutive exponent pp, and the resonance values p=1p=1 and p=1/2p=1/2, at which the particular solution exponent 2/p−12/p-1 coincides with a root of the homogeneous indicial equation and a logarithmic multiplier s2/p−1​ln⁡ss^{2/p-1}\ln s must be introduced, correspond to physically significant conductivity laws that each warrant a focused independent treatment. The spatial framework adopted here, in which the index ν\nu encodes cylindrical or spherical radial symmetry, accurately captures a wide class of physically relevant configurations but does not accommodate angular anisotropy, shear deformation, or non-radial thermal gradients, all of which arise naturally in genuinely multi-dimensional thermoelastic problems. For the cylindrical case ν=1\nu=1 with nonzero flux constant A1A_{1}, the displacement field GB​(z)G_{B}(z) (106) is expressed as a definite integral whose integrand involves the cylindrical thermal profile and does not reduce to standard special functions for arbitrary A1A_{1}, reflecting the intrinsic complexity of the cylindrical Green’s function that makes this case structurally richer than any other geometry.

The exact solutions constructed throughout this work satisfy the governing equations identically, yet the question of whether they attract nearby trajectories of the full nonlinear system or represent isolated exact states requires a separate spectral analysis of the linearised operator about each solution and is not pursued here, as it would constitute a substantial independent investigation. The thermoelastic coupling constants β\beta and γ\gamma and the material density ρ\rho are treated as spatially and thermally uniform throughout; in functionally graded materials or high-temperature processes these parameters may depend on temperature or position, and incorporating such dependence would enrich the constitutive classification by generating additional symmetry branches not present in the current analysis.

Finally, the optimal systems of subalgebras are constructed for generic parameter ranges, deliberately setting aside the degenerate cases p=0p=0, q=0q=0, p+q=0p+q=0, and 2​q−p=02q-p=0, at which adjoint weights vanish and additional inequivalent one-dimensional subalgebras emerge that require the optimal system to be reconstructed entirely from first principles; a complete treatment of all such degenerate branches, together with their associated invariant solutions, represents a well-defined and self-contained extension of the present classification programme.

7 Conclusion

We have constructed a complete constitutive classification of the nonlinearly coupled thermoelastic system (1) and derived exact group-invariant solutions for each admissible constitutive class.

The classification yields three principal branches: the exponential class C=C0​ep​uC=C_{0}e^{pu}, K=K0​eq​uK=K_{0}e^{qu}, E=E0​er​uE=E_{0}e^{ru}; the power-law class C=C0​upC=C_{0}u^{p}, K=K0​u2​pK=K_{0}u^{2p}, E=E0E=E_{0}; and a unified class K=K0​C2K=K_{0}C^{2}, E=E0E=E_{0} that subsumes both as special cases. For each branch, the admitted symmetry algebra is determined, an optimal system of one-dimensional subalgebras is constructed, and representative generators are used to reduce the governing PDEs to coupled ODE systems.

For the exponential class, the scaling reduction with α=1\alpha=1, σ=1/2\sigma=1/2 yields a thermal field described by a logarithmic outer profile u=2​ln⁡(z/t)−2​t2/z2u=2\ln(z/t)-2t^{2}/z^{2} and a displacement field with inverse-distance decay w=8​t3/2/(3​z)w=8t^{3/2}/(3z). The geometry parameter ν\nu is absorbed into the similarity transformation at leading order, so the solution retains the same functional form for both cylindrical and spherical geometries, with the geometric difference confined to a subdominant correction.

For the power-law class, the scaling reduction produces a thermal field u=Az2/pt−1/pu=Az^{2/p}t^{-1/p} and a displacement field decomposed into three physically distinct modes: a steady elastic component C1​z(p+1)/pC_{1}z^{(p+1)/p}, a self-similarly growing homogeneous component C2​z1/p​t1/pC_{2}z^{1/p}t^{1/p}, and a linearly growing thermoelastic coupling term D​z2/p−1​tDz^{2/p-1}t driven by β\beta. The coupling term vanishes identically when β=0\beta=0, confirming that it is a direct signature of the thermoelastic interaction.

For travelling-wave reductions under both the exponential and power-law classes, exact solutions are obtained for ν≠1\nu\neq 1 in elementary closed form involving tanh−1\tanh^{-1} and polynomial functions, while the cylindrical case ν=1\nu=1 introduces a logarithmic correction that requires quadrature when the flux constant A1≠0A_{1}\neq 0. The displacement field for general pp is expressed compactly through the Gauss hypergeometric function F12​(12,−12​p+1,32,λ​z2/A2){}_{2}F_{1}(\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2p+1};\frac{3}{2};\lambda z^{2}/A_{2}), which reduces to a cubic polynomial for p=0p=0 and to a linear function in the isothermal limit p→∞p\to\infty.

Taken together, these results provide a systematic analytical framework for nonlinear thermoelastic systems with temperature-dependent material properties, offering exact benchmarks for numerical methods and explicit descriptions of the dominant physical balances in each constitutive and geometric regime.
